as-dead:
John's response to his vision of the exalted Christ echoes the responses of Ezekiel (1:28, 3:23 & 43:3) & Daniel (8:15-18, 10:7-11). When visited by heavenly messengers &/or 'the glory of the Lord', these OT prophets also fell on their face until 'the Spirit lifted me' or the angelic messenger touched them and 'set me upon my feet.'
John's response, however, is an amplification: Exekiel says 'I fell upon my face', Daniel says 'I fell on my face in a deep sleep' but John says 'I fell at his feet as though dead.' This more extreme response is proportional to the greater revelation of divine presence & glory embodied in the exalted Christ.
It may also be that this experience & account would evoke apostolic memories of the glory of Christ revealed during his ministry that produced similar responses among them of awe & worship (cf. Matt 17:5-6; Luke 5:5-10; 8:22-25; John 21:4-12).
right-hand:
Jesus here repeats the action of the angel Gabriel who 'touched' Daniel & helped him stand (cf. Dan 8:15-18, 10:7-11).
In John's account, though, the hand that touches, reassures & strengthens him is the same authoritative 'right hand' that holds the '7 stars', symbols of the powers of all time & space. Given John's many allusions to Isaiah in the surrounding verses, this image also evokes the promise of Yahweh to his servant in Isaiah 41:10 to 'uphold you with my victorious right hand.' For John, Jesus the cosmic conquering King of Kings is also & forever (just like his Father) the empowering Friend of sinners!
It may be that this experience & account would also evoke apostolic memories of the empowering, enlivening effect of Jesus' touch (cf. Matt 17:1-8; Luke 5:12-13; Luke 7:12-15; Luke 8:49-55; Mark 9:25-27).
fear-not:
Jesus' opening encouragement here to 'fear not' echoes the phrase (& equivalent variants; eg. 'do not fear', 'do not be afraid') used by God, angels & prophets to reassure the people of God throughout the OT.
Again, it is very likely that this account would also evoke apostolic memories of various times when Jesus during his 3 year ministry urged his disciples to 'fear not'.
As Barclay concludes,'Even in heaven, when we come near the unapproachable glory, Jesus is saying: "I am here; do not be afraid."'
fear-not-ot:
[Back]

'Fear not' & equivalent phrases occur in most sections of the OT, with more than 110 specific instances. Representative examples include Genesis 15:1, Exodus 20:20, Deuteronomy 31:6-8, 1 Samuel 12:19-20, 2 Chronicles 20:17, Isaiah 43:5, 54:4 & Zechariah 8:13-15.
Two OT instances with particular relevance to John's experience are Isaiah 41:10 & Daniel 10:10-19, where the words 'fear not' are associated with the strengthening help of God & being upheld by his 'victorious right hand'.
fear-not-gospels:
[Back]

Relevant examples include:
  • When facing persecution or trial: eg. Matt 10:26-31
  • Reassurance of provision & the Kingdom: eg. Luke 12:22-34
  • Miraculous encounters, including:
    • on the way to the house of Jairus (Luke 8:49-50)
    • when Jesus appeared walking on the sea in the midst of a storm (Matthew 14:26-33)
    • when Jesus was transfigured: 'his face shone like the sun' & God spoke 'from the cloud' (Matthew 17:5-8)
    • after the resurrection, both the angel at the tomb & the risen Christ begin their messages to the women with 'do not be afraid' (Matthew 28:5-10)
I-am:
'I am (ἐγώ εἰμι) the first & the last' is a deliberate echo of Isaiah's declaration of Yahweh's exclusive & all-encompassing divinity found in:
  • Isaiah 41:4 - 'I, the Lord, am the first, & with the last I am He'
  • Isaiah 48:12 - 'I am He, I am the first, & I am the last.'
Here, 'I am he' translates אֲנִי הוּא ('ani hu' ≈ ἐγώ εἰμι in LXX ≈ 'egō eimi' ≈ an emphatic 'I am!'). Isaiah is clearly drawing on the more ancient account in which God gives his name to Moses as 'I Am' (Exodus 3:14). The Hebrew phrase, אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה ('Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh' ≈ 'I Am who I Am'), shortened later in the verse to אֶהְיֶה ('Ehyeh', usually pronounced as 'Yahweh' ≈ 'I Am') is also translated in the LXX as ἐγώ εἰμι.
John here in 1:17 is deliberately drawing on these significant OT connections to ascribe this name of Yahweh - with its implications of eternal, uncreated, self-sufficient deity - to the risen Jesus.
first-last:
This title of 'the first & the last' in the OT is an unequivocal self-designation of God, occurring 3 times in Isaiah.
In Revelation, this phrase is closely related to two other divine titles, 'the Alpha & the Omega' (see notes on 1:8) & 'the beginning & the end.'
Taken together, John's ascription of these divine titles to Jesus present him not as a 'second god' (an obscene polytheism for any Jew or Christian in the 1st century) yet nevertheless as somehow integral to the divine nature & identity of Yahweh, Creator God of all the world. This reinforces earlier apostolic statements suggesting that Jesus, a man raised in Nazareth & crucified under Pontius Pilate in Judea around AD 30, somehow shares in the divine & eternal nature of the Heavenly Father (cf. Philipiians 2:5-8, Colossians 2:9, Hebrews 1:2-4), as developed further in the later formulations of trinitarian theology.
first-last-Isaiah:
[Back]

The relevant passages from Isaiah are in the section that seems to directly address the Babylonian exile of Israel, including:
  • 41:4, when Isaiah insists it is Yahweh who has 'stirred up' the Babylonian ruler & his army 'from the east' to take Israel into exile ... Babylon even in its cruel victory over Israel is simply a tool in the hands of Yahweh, Lord of all the earth!
  • 44:6, when Yahweh declares that 'besides me there is no god,' & goes on to ridicule the gods of idolatrous nations like Babylon.
  • 48:12, when Yahweh declares his ultimate power as creator & ruler of the world & cosmos, insisting that he will 'perform his purpose on Babylon, & his arm shall be against the Chaldeans.'
first-last-beginning-end:
[Back]

Here in John's opening vision, Jesus explicitly calls himself 'the first and the last' (1:17). Jesus repeats his claim to this title in John's closing chapter (22:13), where he equates it with two other divine self-designations (cf. 21:5), 'the Alpha & the Omega' (see notes on 1:8) & 'the beginning & the end.'
This last phrase echoes similar usage in the OT which points to the unique & eternal presence & knowledge of Yahweh (cf. Eccl 3:11 & Isaiah 46:8-10). It may also evoke the meditation of the writer of Hebrews (7:1-3, 15-17) regarding Jesus as 'a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek,' the mysterious ancient priest-king of Salem (an early name for Jerusalem) who 'has neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God he continues a priest for ever.'
living-one:
'The living one' is a title which evokes the many OT passages and equivalent number of NT passages which refer to Yahweh as 'the living God'. Jewish apocalyptic writers also used the phrase 'the living one' a few times, & only ever as a title for Yahweh, highlighting his eternal power over life, death, and destiny.
In the NT, Jesus is referred to as 'the living one' (τoν ζῶντα ≈ 'the living' or 'the living one') only here & in one other instance: by the angels at the tomb after the resurrection (Luke 24:5). He is, however, quite frequently identified as the source of eternal life in the world, in the apostolic teachings of John (cf. John 1:4, 5:21-26, 10:10, 11:25-26, 14:6; 1 John 5:11-13), Peter (eg. Acts 3:15) & Paul (eg. Col 3:3).
Given the surrounding verses, John seems to include all these connotations in his use here of 'the living one.'
living-God-ot:
[Back]

'The living God' as a designation for Yahweh often appears at pivotal moments in the OT stories of Israel, including in:
  • the Torah (eg. Deut 5:26)
  • the historical books (eg. Joshua 3:10 & 1 Sam 17:26 ,36)
  • the Psalms (eg. 42:2 & 84:2)
  • the prophets, including:
    • Hosea 1:10
    • Isaiah 37:4, 17
    • Jer 10:10, 23:36
    • Daniel 6:20, 26 (uses an Aramaic equivalent of the Hebrew term)

In addition to these direct titles, God's own name of Yahweh (often translated "I AM who I AM" in Exodus 3:14) carries the fundamental meaning of self-existence and eternal being.
living-God-nt:
[Back]

'The living God' as a designation for the Heavenly Father appears throughout the NT, including in:
  • Matthew, the Gospel intended for Jewish audiences (eg. 16:15-16 where Jesus is 'the Son of the living God', 26:63)
  • Acts (eg. Acts 14:15)
  • the Epistles, including:
    • Paul's letters to:
      • the Thessalonians (1 Thess 1:9)
      • the Corinthans (2 Cor 3:3, 6:16)
      • the Romans (Rom 9:26)
      • Timothy(1 Tim 3:15, 4:10)
    • the letter to the Hebrews, that is, the Jewish Christians! (3:12, 9:14 & 10:31)
  • Revelation (cf. 7:2)

1 John (cf. 5:20) also uses the phrase 'the true God and eternal life' to refer to either Jesus or his Heavenly Father (the grammar is ambiguous).
living-God:
[Back]

This phrase is typically used to highlight:
  • the contrast between Yahweh - in his vitality & creative, revelatory speech - and the dead, mute idols of the ancient empires (not least the Roman Empire of John's time!)
  • life as an essential attribute of Yahweh's eternal nature: he possesses life in Himself & is the sole source of breath for all creation
  • Yahweh's proactive involvement in human history: he is imminent & relational rather than distant or detached
  • Yahweh's presence as intimate & transformative: he 'dwells with' and 'walks among' His people, transforming them into His 'living temple.'
  • Yahweh's absolute sovereignty as king & judge of the world
living-one-JAL:
[Back]

'The living one' was only used a few times by the Jewish apocalyptic writers, usually as a designation for Yahweh in his role as Heavenly King & Judge. Examples include:
  • 1 Enoch 47:3 (~ 100 BC) - 'I saw him - the Antecedent of Time, while he was sitting upon the throne of his glory, and the books of the living one were open before him' (based on modern critical versions of 1 Enoch, not less scholarly online versions that render the relevant phrase as 'the books of the living').
  • The Testament of Abraham 2:18 (late 1st C AD) - Yahweh sends instructions through Michael using formulas like: 'Thus says the Living One ...' or 'Go, say to the righteous Abraham, by the word of the Living One ...'
  • The Greek Apocalypse of Ezra 2:18 (~ 2nd C AD?) - 'And Ezra said: 'How can I stand before the judgment seat of the Living One?'
died:
This direct reference to the death of Jesus is a little startling here! 'The living one' who is 'alive for evermore' ... died!?
All 4 Gospels (Matthew 27:26-35, Mark 15:15-24, Luke 23:25-33, John 19:15-18) make it clear Pilate, the Roman Prefect of Judea, appointed & acting under Caesar's authority, 'delivered Jesus up' to his Roman soldiers to be crucified on a Roman cross, the empire's signature form of execution for non-citizens. John's later visions in Revelation will symbolically re-tell story of when Rome's beastly political & military system (& the Satanic powers acting through them) set out to kill & bury this Jesus for good - the same system now in John's day directed in many ways against the churches.
Rome actually succeeded, of course, apparantly defeating the Lamb of God - he died, like all those dead-&-deified emperors from Augustus to Domitian's deceased son. Yet unlike them, Jesus did not stay dead! Here he is, some 60 years later looking more alive - more like Life itself - than anyone John had ever encountered, remembering almost off-handedly that time 'I died.'
alive-evermore:
ζῶν εἰμι εἰς τους αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων (literally, 'I am alive into the ages of the ages') is often assumed to be about a life that extends into the unending future (as implied by translations with terms like 'for evermore' & 'eternally'). In NT usage, however, ζωη αἰώνιος ('zōē aiōnios' ≈ 'life of the age') was not simply 'life unending', but rather a certain quality of life that will be experienced by all when the reign of God is re-established in individual lives, communities and throughout the world - the life of 'the age to come' (cf. Mark 29:30, Hebrews 4:5) which was expected to begin after the Final Judgement.
Here, then, Jesus is declaring that he has passed through death & resurrection into the 'life of the ages of the ages', the fulness of a new type & quality of life now available through his victory to all who follow him.
alive-evermore-nt:
[Back]

The NT writers shared the Jewish perspective which regards this current era of human experience in which we live (since the time of the Fall until the future coming in fulness of the reign of God in the world) as 'this present evil age' (cf. Gal 1:4). They looked forward to a time when all sin, evil & suffering would be ended & universal shalom re-established under the perfect kingdom of God ... 'the age to come'.
In John's Gospel, though, Jesus radically suggested this 'life of the age (to come)' could be entered into now - in the midst of 'this present evil age' - by those who trust & follow him (cf. 3:36, 5:24). For Jesus-followers, then, the future resurrection on 'the last day' will simply be the physical finalisation of a spiritual reality that has already occurred (cf. 6:40). For Jesus, this 'life of the age (to come)' is not primarily about immortal existence, but about an unbroken intimate union & fellowship with the Father & the Son (cf. 17:3).
Of course, union with the ultimate source of Life by implication means immortality - as CS Lewis put it: 'Once a man is united to God, how could he not live forever?' But the key quality of eternal life is union with the Father & the Son, & hence with each other (cf. John 17:20-23).
